items.title: Cursor loses OpenAI model access on November 12 — two days away; GPT models wind down after SpaceX's acquisition of Anysphere, with Grok Build and the Cursor Models pool positioned as the replacement path
items.summary: OpenAI told SpaceX on August 28, 2026, that it intends to wind down Cursor's contract for OpenAI models, proposing a November 12, 2026 shutoff — now two days from this snapshot. OpenAI described it as the maximum notice permitted under the contract, which includes a change-of-ownership termination window. The trigger is SpaceX's $60 billion all-stock acquisition of Anysphere (Cursor's parent), announced June 16, 2026 and closed in August. OpenAI's stated concern is distillation and terms-of-service compliance: it points to Musk's sworn admission that xAI 'partly' used OpenAI output in training, and says it cannot be confident SpaceX will use OpenAI's technology within terms. There is no public evidence that Cursor itself passed OpenAI outputs into the SpaceXAI or Grok training pipeline. Cursor's CEO has said OpenAI models account for roughly 5% of Cursor's user traffic — the majority of Cursor usage goes to Anthropic and Google models, plus SpaceXAI's Grok models and Cursor's own in-house models (Composer). After the shutoff: Cursor will continue to offer Anthropic (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.2 pending availability), Google (Gemini), the SpaceXAI Grok family (Grok 4.5, Grok 4.6 — both reportedly developed using Cursor's own usage data under the new ownership), and Grok Build, SpaceXAI's own coding agent that is being pushed inside the Cursor platform. One secondary source cites Cursor pricing for Grok at roughly $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for the standard tier, with faster variants higher; Cursor has also moved Grok and Composer into a 'Cursor Models' pool with substantially more included usage on paid plans. Future OpenAI models — Astra (GPT-6 family) and anything after — will not be added to Cursor. The shutoff does not affect Cursor's pricing structure or Privacy Mode directly, both of which are governed by Cursor's own terms rather than OpenAI's.
items.why_it_matters: This is one of the first concrete cases of a frontier-lab API contract being terminated specifically because of who owns the downstream company, not because of any proven misuse. For any developer using Cursor in day-to-day work, the practical effect is immediate: if you currently route Cursor at GPT-5.5, GPT-6, or any OpenAI model through the built-in model picker, that selector stops working on November 12. The honest default migration path is to Anthropic or Google models in Cursor — Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 are both high-end coding options, and Gemini 3.5 and the Gemini Omni family are available for cases where you want a different style. Grok Build is being pushed as the SpaceX-native replacement, and it is fine as a coding model (the Artificial Analysis benchmarks from July put Grok 4.5 in competitive range for coding tasks), but relying on it means your coding stack now runs on a model trained by a company whose incentives are partially about not losing the Cursor install base — a reasonable choice, but one worth making consciously. The structural lesson for anyone building on frontier-lab APIs is the one Rohit Krishnan and several others flagged: model access is now an M&A risk. If you are depending on a particular lab's API as a bottleneck in your product or workflow, a change in ownership on the upstream side — or a change in terms of service on the downstream side — can terminate that access with as little as ~75 days' notice. For a hobbyist using Cursor on personal projects, this doesn't require anything more than swapping the default model. For anyone building a Claude Code mod, an MCP server, or a Python wrapper around the Anthropic or OpenAI API, the lesson is to build the switch between providers at the configuration level — not at the API-call level. The broader signal is that OpenAI and SpaceXAI are now publicly treating each other as competitors rather than partners, which matters for the pace of future model availability across neutral developer platforms: Cursor, which had been the clearest 'any frontier model' developer environment, is now effectively a non-OpenAI environment. Expect the same dynamic to show up in other developer tools over the next 6–12 months.
items.why_it_matters_brief: OpenAI's November 12 cutoff of Cursor's GPT access is 48 hours away — model access is now an M&A risk, and the honest migration for anyone using the OpenAI picker in Cursor is to Anthropic or Google, not Grok.

items.title: Thinking Machines Lab ships Inkling 2 Small — a 594B/17B-active MoE on Tinker with Apache 2.0 weights promised for next week; scores 31 on Artificial Analysis vs 13 for the predecessor
items.summary: On November 5, 2026, Thinking Machines Lab — the AI lab founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati — released Inkling 2 Small, its second model and the successor to July's Inkling Small. Inkling 2 Small is a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active per token, image-input capable, and launched with closed weights on Tinker (the lab's inference and fine-tuning platform). Murati said at launch that the model is 'live on Tinker today' and that the lab plans to release the weights under Apache 2.0 'next week' after external safety testing and red-teaming — so the weights release is pending and not yet confirmed as of this snapshot. On Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, the lab reports Inkling 2 Small scoring 31, up from 13 for the smaller first Inkling (276B total / 12B active, released July 30, 2026, Apache 2.0). Artificial Analysis's write-up reportedly places Inkling 2 Small in the range of 'matches Google DeepMind's Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and surpasses Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6-Pro' on its Intelligence Index — those are the lab's own framing of the external ranking, and the Artificial Analysis page lists the model as proprietary at launch, with the Apache 2.0 weights release planned. The lab is positioning Inkling 2 Small against three segments: (1) frontier coding models, where Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 are the comparison; (2) open-weight MoEs from Chinese labs (DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B); and (3) US-origin open-weight options, which the lab frames as a competitive gap versus Chinese labs. Output-token price on Tinker is reportedly 75% below Inkling Small's launch price, though Thinking Machines has not published a full pricing table on its website. One concrete caveat worth carrying: at 594B total parameters the full weights will be a ~532GB download, which puts them out of reach for anyone without serious hardware for anything beyond quantized local inference — this is an enterprise and research release, not a hobbyist one.
items.why_it_matters: Inkling 2 Small is relevant mainly for two reasons that aren't about the headline score. First, it is one of the few serious US-built open-weight releases of the year. Over the past six months, the center of gravity for open-weight frontier models has moved to Chinese labs — DeepSeek, Moonshot (Kimi K3), Alibaba (Qwen3.8), MiniMax — because US frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) have moved steadily closed. Thinking Machines is explicitly trying to fill that gap with a US-origin team and a US-origin model under Apache 2.0, which in licensing terms is close to the most permissive possible — no revenue thresholds, no field-of-use restrictions, no 'commercial use requires separate license' clause. If the weights land next week as promised, it will be the first serious open-weight US frontier-tier model released since Mistral Large 4 in late October (which is French/EU, not US), and the first sub-trillion-parameter-count model that credibly competes on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index from a US team. Second, the Tinker-first access pattern is worth noticing on its own. Thinking Machines is running a setup where weights eventually ship under Apache 2.0, but inference-time and fine-tuning access is first-class on Tinker, their platform. That is a different business model from Hugging Face's 'weights are the product, you figure out hosting' approach — it's closer to how Mistral runs La Plateforme or how Together AI runs its serving layer. The practical implication: a developer who wants to try Inkling 2 Small can hit Tinker today with no infrastructure work; a team that wants to self-host needs to wait for the weights. For Gabe specifically, there are two actionable pieces. First, if you want to try an open-weight US-origin model with a real benchmark score without setting up local inference, Tinker is the current path — their API wraps the model, their Jupyter integration lets you call it from a Python notebook. Second, if the Apache 2.0 weights land next week, this is one to put on the watchlist as a candidate for small-scale fine-tuning projects: the architecture is a standard MoE and the weights will be usable through any inference stack that supports MoE models (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp with the right quantization). The caveat is the ~532GB download — real local inference needs serious GPU budget, but quantized inference on a decent consumer workstation is possible. Third, this release is a direct signal of how the 'open-weight gap' is being filled: not by one big US lab releasing frontier weights, but by Murati's post-OpenAI team positioning a US alternative between the closed frontier and the Chinese open-weight stack.

items.title: Claude Code v2.1.317 ships the gateway cost report API and blocking Agent SDK hook callbacks — the control-plane piece behind last week's Anthropic Enterprise Security Center bundle
items.summary: Anthropic shipped Claude Code v2.1.317 on or around November 2, 2026. Two changes matter from the release notes. First, the Claude apps gateway gets a new admin API for cost reporting: GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost returns past spend over a configurable date range, broken out by total, developer, day, or identity-provider group. This is the operational data an enterprise admin needs to run a Claude Code deployment with a budget — before this, usage visibility was per-session or per-user but not aggregated server-side. The endpoint is admin-only (organization:manage permission) and ties into the same Enterprise Security Center product that went to beta on November 5 — the cost API is the data-pull mechanism behind the Security Center's budget-tracking panels. Second, failed Agent SDK hook callbacks can now block the action they wrap. This is the SDK-level counterpart to the Claude Code v2.1.295 change from October 9 that added onFailure: 'block' to command and HTTP hooks: if a hook callback registered via the Agent SDK fails to return, times out, or raises, the tool call it intercepts is now blocked rather than silently allowed through. Combined with v2.1.295, the pattern across Anthropic's whole hook surface — command hooks, HTTP hooks, SDK callbacks, and inference hooks at the API layer — is now 'hook failure fails closed, decision is logged.' The release also includes a user-facing change: a prompt before a tool call sends the account email address over the network, intended to catch cases where an outbound tool (e.g., a webhook or external API call) would leak the account owner's identity without explicit confirmation. Third-party aggregators also mention v2.1.318 (November 3, 2026) addressing sign-in expiry warnings and config writes, though that release is cosmetic and operational rather than a capability change. Neither v2.1.317 nor v2.1.318 changes the SDK's public API surface — hook signatures, tool-definition shapes, and the agent loop are unchanged. The release is backward-compatible for existing hooks that don't opt into the new blocking behavior.
items.why_it_matters: Two things in this release matter directly for anyone writing Claude Code mods or wrapping the Agent SDK in Python. First, the blocking-hook-callback change is the SDK-level completion of the pattern Anthropic has been building toward since September: hooks are no longer advisory, they are enforcing. If you register an SDK hook that checks whether a tool call touches a sensitive file, a credential, or an external URL, and that hook returns deny or fails to return, the tool call is blocked, logged, and surfaced to the user. For a Claude Code mod that sits between the model and the filesystem (or between the model and the network), this is the point where the 'guardrail' framing becomes real: you can now enforce invariants that the model cannot bypass by rephrasing or retrying. The design lesson that is now consistent across Anthropic's whole stack — command hooks, HTTP hooks, SDK callbacks, inference hooks — is to design for fail-closed: if the hook cannot decide, the action does not happen. For a hobbyist, the useful version of this is: wrap any tool call that touches a filesystem path, a shell command, or a network URL in an SDK hook that validates the target, and trust that a failure in the hook cannot leak through. Second, the gateway cost API is the thing that unlocks real spend governance in team environments. Before this, running Claude Code across a team meant either accepting that spend tracking was per-user (visible in the Anthropic console, not in your own observability stack), or running your own gateway and tracking spend at that layer. The new endpoint is pullable from any dashboarding stack that can hit an HTTP API with a bearer token — LangSmith, Langfuse, Grafana, Datadog — and the breakdown by developer, day, or IdP group is the operational data a budget owner actually needs. For a solo developer this is mostly background information, but it matters because it is one of the two pieces (the other being the Security Center) that make 'run Claude Code across a team with a shared budget' a one-dashboard operation rather than a scripts-and-CSVs problem. The structural read is that Anthropic's enterprise stack is now caught up with OpenAI's — the gaps around admin tooling, spend visibility, and enforceable policy that were real in mid-2026 have been closed by the October and November releases.

items.title: NVIDIA shows a GR00T teaser at CoRL 2026 in Austin — Jim Fan's keynote week confirms real humanoid hardware operating autonomously at normal speed, no post-event write-ups yet
items.summary: The Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026 is running November 9–12, 2026, in Austin, Texas, with the main conference on November 9–11 and workshops on November 12. NVIDIA is a major presence this year as it has been for the past three CoRLs, and Jim Fan — co-lead of Project GR00T and distinguished scientist at NVIDIA — is giving the keynote. The pre-conference teaser Fan posted, confirmed via Crypto Briefing's coverage, shows real humanoid hardware operating autonomously at normal human speed with no human operator or teleoperation. That is a different claim than most prior humanoid demos — the standard pattern has been a teleoperated or slowed-down rig, with the autonomy claims made in simulation or on isolated subtasks. The teaser's two interesting elements are (1) 'real hardware' (not sim-to-real pending), and (2) 'normal speed' (not slowed down to accommodate inference latency). CoRL's official site confirms the Austin dates and the keynote structure: presentations and keynotes on Days 1 and 2 are at the Hilton Austin; the reception and Day 3 keynote are at Bass Hall. Some outlets report Fan's keynote is on November 9 (opening), others on Day 3 (November 11) at Bass Hall. As of this snapshot, no post-event coverage has surfaced that confirms what Fan actually showed on stage — the teaser is where the information currently stops. Context on NVIDIA's GR00T status: at CoRL 2025 in Seoul, NVIDIA announced GR00T N1.6 (open reasoning VLA model, integrates Cosmos Reason) and the Newton physics engine inside Isaac Lab. At GTC Taipei (June 1, 2026), NVIDIA announced the Isaac GR00T Reference Humanoid Robot for academic research — the same reference-design body platform that is now expected to be the hardware target of the new autonomy claims. On November 5, 2026 (in today's am snapshot), NVIDIA also released four open-weight Cosmos 3 checkpoints — two scene-level, one policy-level, one joint — which are the world-simulation complement to the physical-robot side of the GR00T stack.
items.why_it_matters: This is one for the watchlist, not the newsflash column. Humanoid robotics has been the AI subfield with the highest ratio of impressive demos to shipping product over the past three years — from Figure 01 and Figure 02, to Tesla's Optimus, to Unitree G1, to Agility Digit, every lab has posted a video that looked like it mattered and most have not translated into usable autonomy. The distinction worth paying attention to on NVIDIA's claim is 'real hardware, normal speed, autonomous' — all three together is the specific combination that would mark a real inflection, because each one on its own has already been demonstrated repeatedly. For Gabe, this is not a stack-adjacent story — HTML/CSS/Python is a long way from humanoid control. But two threads are worth noting. First, NVIDIA's physical-AI stack (Cosmos 3 checkpoints released November 5, GR00T N1.6 at CoRL 2025, Isaac Lab + Newton physics engine) is converging into a single integrated pipeline: world simulator → policy model → real hardware. If the CoRL 2026 keynote closes that loop with an on-stage demo rather than a sim video, it would be the clearest evidence so far that the pipeline actually works end-to-end. Second, the open-weight angle here is unusual for the humanoid space. NVIDIA is publishing the Cosmos 3 checkpoints under OpenMDW 1.1 (confirmed Nov 5 in am), which means independent labs can pretrain policies against NVIDIA's world simulator rather than build one from scratch. If the GR00T reference humanoid platform also stays open-sourced (which was the June 2026 framing at GTC Taipei), the result over 12–18 months would be that academic and small-industry robotics labs have a credible open hardware-plus-model stack, instead of needing a Figure/Tesla/Nuro-scale budget to do humanoid work. The caveat is that the teaser is the only thing anyone has seen as of this snapshot — Fan's actual keynote may or may not deliver the thing the teaser frames. Expect post-event coverage in the next 48 hours (by Nov 11–12), which is the right time to re-evaluate. Treat the 'real hardware, normal speed, autonomous' claim as unverified until the keynote actually runs.

items.title: Anthropic signed a $3.4B deal in late September for 1.7GW of Caterpillar gas generators via OnePWR Solutions — the biggest known single buy of power kit by an AI company, surfaced in FT reporting November 8
items.summary: The Financial Times reported on Sunday, November 8, 2026, that Anthropic agreed to pay approximately $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty, gas-fired generators to power its data centers. The deal was signed in late September with OnePWR Solutions, a power supplier based in San Antonio, Texas. The structure is unusual: rather than Anthropic buying power from OnePWR, Anthropic took over OnePWR's existing orders for Caterpillar generators — kit OnePWR had ordered from Caterpillar about two years earlier but could not complete the purchase on. Anthropic is also taking over the engineering and construction work to install the generators. The FT describes it as the biggest known single buy of power equipment by an AI company. The generators are gas-fired (rather than renewable or grid-connected), which carries emissions and air-permit implications — the FT and other coverage note the comparison to xAI's gas turbines near Memphis, which drew an NAACP lawsuit over air quality. Anthropic's amended S-1 IPO filing (covered as a separate item in today's am snapshot) shows approximately $895 billion in mostly-compute-and-infrastructure commitments, and warns that competing demand for gas supply and pipeline capacity could push local prices higher and make firm fuel contracts harder to secure for Anthropic's planned sites. The deal is a concrete data point behind the OpenAI/Anthropic 'fight for compute' narrative that The Batch (DeepLearning.AI) also covered this week: both frontier labs are buying their way out of the power crunch with large, upfront, non-grid power commitments. The $3.4B figure itself was name-dropped in the OpenAI valuation story in today's am snapshot (the am item mentioned 'the broader backdrop of OpenAI's reported $3.4 billion in power-generator orders for new data centers'), but that framing was wrong — the $3.4B is Anthropic's, not OpenAI's. This pm item corrects the attribution and provides the full detail.
items.why_it_matters: This is a business-section story more than a technical one, but the operational detail is worth understanding because it sets context for how frontier labs will scale capacity through 2027–2028. First, the $3.4B/1.7GW figure converts to roughly $2 per watt of installed capacity, which is on the low end for industrial gas-fired generation — Anthropic is getting kit that OnePWR had already ordered and partially paid for, so the price reflects a distressed-seller takeover more than a market-rate equipment deal. The operational point: the labs are not just buying GPUs anymore, they are buying the power infrastructure to run them, and the power infrastructure takes 18–36 months to build out even when the generators themselves are in hand. Second, the gas-fired choice is the important detail, because it is the honest version of what every lab is actually doing: when a lab says 'we are building a data center,' the underlying power source over the next 24 months is almost certainly gas or diesel generators, not grid renewables — grid connections for new 1GW-plus loads take 4–7 years in most US regions, and labs cannot wait. For Gabe, this is not a stack-adjacent story, but it does matter for understanding the broader economics: the reason API prices for Claude are falling (Fable 5.2 at $8/$40 vs Fable 5.1 at $10/$50) is partly that Anthropic is locking in power infrastructure costs at scale, which reduces the marginal cost per token over the amortization period of the generator fleet. Third, the emissions footprint of this is real and underreported. 1.7GW of gas-fired generation running at typical capacity factors is the same emissions as a small US state, and the labs are concentrating this capacity geographically (Anthropic is building primarily in Texas and the Southwest per the S-1 filing). That is a trade-off the industry is making publicly: the labs are choosing time-to-online over lower emissions. Expect the next 12 months to produce environmental-permitting fights similar to the xAI/Memphis case in multiple jurisdictions. The attribution-correction detail — the $3.4B is Anthropic's, not OpenAI's — matters for anyone trying to track where each lab is spending: Anthropic is heavier on power infrastructure commitments relative to its revenue (about 14% of its planned $895B commitment pool), while OpenAI is heavier on compute lease arrangements (Oracle, Microsoft) and planned power-plant construction rather than generator takeovers.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Anthropic's $3.4B/1.7GW gas-generator deal with OnePWR — the biggest known AI power-kit buy — is the honest version of how frontier labs scale capacity: not renewables, not grid, but gas running at scale for 18–36 months while permanent sites get built.
